newsitem.title: ITALY: Hizbollah leader says Pope will be safe in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Hizbollah leader says Pope will be safe in Lebanon.

text.p: The spiritual leader of Lebanon's pro-Iranian Moslem fundamentalist Hizbollah said in a newspaper interview on Friday that Pope John Paul would not be at risk during his weekend visit to the country.

"We are waiting for this visit with hearts filled with love and minds open to dialogue. The Holy Father has nothing to fear in Lebanon," Sheikh Mohammed Hussein Fadlallah told La Repubblica newspaper.

"We have been waiting for the Holy Father a long time. Of course, a one-day trip cannot solve the political and religious problems of Lebanon...which may need decades to work out, but we have to start somewhere," Fadlallah said.
"We are waiting for the visit with an open mind because it will help us to find here in Lebanon a better way for Moslems and Christians to live side by side," he added.
The Pope, 76, is expected during his 32-hour visit to Beirut to call for reconciliation among Christians and Moslems in Lebanon, where civil war raged from 1975 to 1990.
He cancelled a five-day visit in 1994 over security concerns after the bombing of a Maronite Christian church north of Beirut in which 11 Sunday worshippers were killed and 59 injured.
Security will be high for this weekend's visit, the Pope's first to the Middle East and one month after an apparent assassination attempt during his trip to Sarajevo.
Hours before the Pope arrived in the Bosnian capital, police dismantled anti-tank mines found planted under a bridge on his route from the airport.

Hizbollah (Party of God), a Shi'ite movement, runs welfare programmes in Beirut while fighting a guerrilla war to oust Israeli troops from south Lebanon, where Israel holds a strip comprising about 12 percent of Lebanese territory.
Fadlallah called on the Pontiff to condemn the Israeli presence during his visit.

"We would like the Pope, like Jesus when he chased the merchants from the Temple, to call for the end to Israeli occupation of the south of our country and of Jerusalem, taken over and colonised by Jews," he said.
"The Pope cannot close his eyes in front of this tragedy. We are asking him for an act of courage so that the sweetness of his words don't disappear with the biterness of reality."
Catholic bishops at a Vatican synod in 1995 called openly for the withdrawal of Israeli forces and Syrian troops, about 35,000 of whom are stationed in Lebanon.
